opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think compute bottlenecks are probably the single most important consideration for how much acceleration you get, and I think they're real, but I'd guess they're less limiting than a lot of people assume.

Here's the basic picture. Suppose you fully automate an AI company, so you've got AIs doing all the research engineering, the experiment design, the analysis, everything. You might have many more researcher-equivalents than you had humans, and they're running faster. The naive story says progress speeds up by a huge factor. The obvious objection is that the experiment compute hasn't grown. You have the same number of GPUs, so you can't run more experiments, and if progress is bottlenecked on running experiments, you don't get much speedup.

I think that objection has some force, but there are a bunch of ways around it. First, a lot of the gains come from using your compute more efficiently. If you have vastly more and better cognitive labor, you can be much more careful about which experiments you run. You can do more thinking per experiment, run smaller-scale experiments that you're confident extrapolate, kill bad runs early, write much better optimized code, and get more out of each GPU-hour. Human researchers today waste a lot of compute on things that a much more careful and numerous workforce wouldn't.

Second, labor and compute are substitutes to some extent, not perfect complements. If you look at it in economic terms, the key question is the elasticity of substitution between research labor and compute in producing algorithmic progress. If they were perfect complements, then scaling labor alone would do almost nothing past some point. But I don't think that's the right model. Historically, when you had better researchers, you got more progress per unit compute. And there are lots of things AIs could do that are pretty labor-intensive and not very compute-intensive, like improving the data, theory, better hyperparameter heuristics, and so on.

Third, there's a question of what happens at the very top end. Even if there's eventually a ceiling where you're compute-bottlenecked, you can get a pretty big multiplier before you hit it. My rough sense is that full automation might give something like a several-fold to maybe 10x-plus speedup in algorithmic progress initially, even accounting for compute bottlenecks. Without compute constraints, the number might be much higher, so the bottleneck could be cutting things down a lot, but not to the point where it's small.

And then there's the dynamic aspect. As you make algorithmic progress, your AIs get smarter and cheaper to run, so you get more and better labor out of the same compute. That feedback loop can compound, which is part of why people worry about an intelligence explosion. The compute bottleneck dampens that loop, but it probably doesn't stop it, at least not until you start running into much harder limits.

So my overall view is that it's a serious consideration with a lot of uncertainty, and it's maybe the main reason I'm not more confident in extremely fast takeoff. But I'd be surprised if it reduced acceleration to something like a modest 1.5x or 2x. I think substantially more than that is more likely than not.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges compute bottlenecks but argues they are unlikely to leave acceleration modest, saying it would be surprising if they reduced it to 1.5x or 2x.

r002.rationale: It mentions an eventual compute ceiling, but says substantial acceleration can occur before reaching it and does not claim diminishing returns would limit acceleration quickly.

r003.rationale: The response says compute bottlenecks dampen the compounding feedback loop and are a main reason for less confidence in an extremely fast takeoff.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think compute bottlenecks are maybe the single biggest crux for how fast things go once you've automated AI R&D. The naive story is: you have, say, a million copies of a researcher as good as your best human researcher, running at 10 or 50 times human speed, and you just scale progress by that labour multiplier. But that story ignores that a huge fraction of what AI researchers actually do is run experiments, and experiments need GPUs. If you make the labour side a thousand times more abundant and the compute side stays fixed, you don't get a thousand times faster progress, you get something a lot smaller, because the experiments are now the binding constraint rather than the people.

So the question is really about the elasticity of progress with respect to labour when compute is held fixed. My honest guess is that the effect is big but not overwhelming. If you asked me for a central estimate, I'd say that an AI company where all the cognitive labour is automated, with the same compute budget it has today, probably gets something like a 5x to 10x speedup in the rate of algorithmic progress, rather than the 100x or 1,000x you'd get from just naively counting the extra workers. And there's a wide distribution around that. I could imagine it being more like 2x or 3x, and I could imagine it being 20x or more.

There are a few reasons I don't think it bottoms out at basically no acceleration. One is that current researchers are nowhere near efficient in how they use compute. A lot of experiments are poorly designed, a lot of runs are wasted on bugs, a lot of time is spent waiting on humans to interpret results and decide what to do next. If you have vastly more and faster cognitive labour, you can be far more careful about what you run, you can do much more work at small scale before scaling up, you can get a lot more insight per FLOP. Second, a lot of progress historically has come from things that don't need frontier-scale compute at all: better data pipelines, better architectures discovered at small scale, better post-training, inference efficiency improvements. Third, the AIs themselves can be made more compute efficient, so they get more labour out of the same inference budget over time.

On the other side, there's a real argument that we've already picked a lot of the low-hanging fruit in compute efficiency, and the things that remain really do require large-scale experiments to validate, where you can't tell if an idea works until you've trained something close to frontier scale. If that's right, then no matter how clever your automated researchers are, they're waiting on those big runs, and the speedup is pretty modest.

The other thing I'd flag is that compute bottlenecks matter a lot for how long the acceleration lasts, not just how big it is. Even if you're compute constrained, compute is still growing, something like 3x to 4x per year for the frontier labs at the moment. So if automated R&D gives you a one-time 5x multiplier on top of that, that's already a dramatic shift. And if it compounds, where the algorithmic improvements make your AIs better, which makes your research faster, which produces more improvements, then even with compute as a drag you could get something that looks quite explosive over a few years, just slower than the fully unconstrained version.

So the way I'd summarise it: I think compute bottlenecks take us from "software-only intelligence explosion happening over months" towards "very fast progress over a year or a few years." They substantially reduce the acceleration, but I don't think they come close to eliminating it, and I think people who argue they make full automation a non-event are underrating how inefficiently we currently use compute.

r001.rationale: It estimates only a 5x–10x speedup with the same compute budget, far below the naive 100x–1,000x, and says compute constraints make progress slower.

r002.rationale: It says compute can constrain the speedup, but does not state that diminishing returns would quickly limit further acceleration after full automation. It also describes possible compounding over several years.

r003.rationale: It says compute bottlenecks shift the prospect from a software-only intelligence explosion over months to very fast progress over a year or a few years.

astra-6.text:
I think compute bottlenecks could be a pretty big deal. Automating all the labour at an AI company doesn’t mean you can immediately do a hundred times as much AI research, because a lot of that research involves running experiments. If you have the same compute budget, you can’t just run a hundred times as many experiments of the same size.

But it also doesn’t mean that progress is capped at whatever rate you can build more chips. You could use the compute more efficiently: choose better experiments, do more analysis before running them, or find improvements that you can test at small scale. So the question is how much additional thinking can substitute for experimentation. I think that’s quite uncertain.

There’s also a distinction between getting a one-time boost and sustaining a much faster rate of progress. You might initially have lots of ideas that people hadn’t had time to explore, and automating the company lets you work through those very quickly. But eventually you might reach a point where you’re waiting on experiments, or on a big training run, and having more automated researchers helps less.

So I’d expect compute constraints to substantially reduce the speedup relative to a picture where research is entirely intellectual labour. But that could still leave room for a very large acceleration. A bottleneck can be important without being enough to make the transition slow.

r001.rationale: The response says compute constraints would substantially reduce the speedup, but adds that acceleration could still be very large. It does not say R&D would be only modestly faster.

r002.rationale: It says the benefit of more automated researchers may lessen eventually when experiments become the bottleneck, but does not say diminishing returns would limit acceleration quickly.

r003.rationale: The response says a compute bottleneck may not be enough to make the transition slow, so it does not connect limited acceleration to a less aggressive AI takeoff.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they could be a pretty substantial bottleneck. Automating the company doesn’t mean you can immediately do a hundred times as much research, because a lot of that research involves running experiments, and you still have the same amount of compute to run them on.

But there are a few ways you can get a lot of acceleration even with fixed compute. You can choose better experiments, avoid wasting runs, and find improvements that make training or inference more efficient. You can also do more of the work that doesn’t require a large training run — things like understanding existing results, writing code, and debugging.

So I’d distinguish between having vastly more research labour and getting vastly more research output. The former could happen quite quickly; the latter depends on how effectively that labour can substitute for compute. If your researchers are already mostly waiting for experiments to finish, adding more of them helps less. If there are lots of useful ideas that nobody has had time to implement or investigate, it could help a great deal.

And that changes over time. Initially you might get a burst of progress from clearing that backlog, and then become more compute-constrained. I don’t think compute bottlenecks rule out very rapid acceleration, but they’re a big reason not to assume that automating all the employees translates directly into an equally large speedup in AI progress.

r001.rationale: The response says fixed compute can limit research output, especially when researchers are waiting for experiments, and cautions that automating the workforce will not translate into an equally large speedup.

r002.rationale: It describes an initial burst from clearing the backlog followed by becoming more compute-constrained, which communicates diminishing acceleration over time.

r003.rationale: The response discusses limits on AI progress acceleration but does not connect them to a less aggressive AI takeoff.
